newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE says Albania future in hands of the voters.
newsitem.headline: OSCE says Albania future in hands of the voters.

text.p: Leaders of Europe's security forum involved in organising elections in Albania signalled on Wednesday that the polls might not be perfect but said they were the best chance of securing democracy in the lawless state.

Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, current chairman of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said the June 29 polls were indispensable for Albania to start building a lasting democracy.

"These are not going to be easy elections. But if Albania is to start to build democratic structures...these elections are absolutely necessary," Petersen told a news conference after a day of meetings at OSCE headquarters in Vienna.
He dismissed suggestions that the international community had forced Albania's political parties into agreeing to hold the elections too soon.

He also disagreed with a reporter's question that the OSCE's political leaders had ignored the advice of the organisation's election experts to delay the poll to avoid the kind of manipulation that marred last year's general election.
"It was at the request of Albania's political parties that the election should be held," Petersen added.

Hundreds of observers from the 54-nation OSCE and hundreds more from the Council of Europe -- set up to monitor democracy and human rights in Europe -- will be present during the elections and will be escorted by an Italian-led multinational protection force already stationed in the Balkan state.

Petersen, who earlier met the OSCE's special envoy to Albania Franz Vranitzky and the foreign ministers of Switzerland and Poland, made a special plea to Albanian authorities to allow polling stations to close early. Current election law requires the polls to stay open till 9 p.m. -- nearly nightfall.
Opposition parties have also called for polling to close early to minimise the risks of late voting and an after-dark count in a country where armed gangs roam towns at night.
"It would be an advantage...and would give the OSCE a fair chance of observing the counting," Petersen said.

Vranitzky criticised Albanian election organisers for being too slow in meeting targets for candidate lists, which he said was delaying the printing of ballot papers. Around 50 percent of candidates' names had so far been received, he said.

He told the news conference that the OSCE had realistic expectations of the elections, and that it did not foresee an immediate return to law and order or that thousands of looted guns and ammunition would be collected.
Once a new government is formed, it has to put its own house in order and also cooperate with the international community to restore the economy and social and financial infrastructures, he added.
"This is a complicated, even a risky, operation...but the future of the country is the responsibility of those who live there," Vranitzky said.
Catherine Lalumiere, who will be in charge of certifying the elections, said an election held under military protection could not be considered to be very democratic.
"We know the situation in Albania is abnormal and does not meet all the criteria of a democracy..but if these elections go off fairly well, that in itself will be a success," she said.
Lalumiere said she would make an announcement on the conduct of the first round of the vote on the late afternoon or early evening of Monday, June 30. The second round takes place on July 6.
